title: Typed-fragment choreography: acceptance criteria for incremental envelopes, tool invocation orchestration, and repair flows
creator: Aisha Raman
body:
Context:
We need a deterministic, debuggable contract for streaming structured responses that interleave typed fragments (envelopes/frames) and tool/function calls. This ticket captures acceptance criteria, operational requirements, and example test cases for the product + engineering teams to implement the "typed-fragment choreography" pattern across hosted and private deployments.

Goals:
- Define what a minimal, typed fragment looks like (envelope headers, sequence ids, frame types).
- Specify semantics for tool/function invocation messages vs content frames and how clients should reconcile partial state.
- Specify failure and repair modes (truncation, duplication, ordering gaps) and deterministic recovery behaviors.
- Provide acceptance tests and telemetry requirements to validate regressions.

Non-goals:
- This ticket is not a full protocol RFC (that lives in apis/specs). It focuses on acceptance criteria for product and QA for the runtime and console integrations.

Acceptance criteria (high level):
1) Envelope/Frame contract: every emitted frame MUST include these ASCII headers encoded in the transport metadata: type, seq_id, parent_id (optional), payload_schema (optional), and is_final (boolean). Payloads may be JSON objects or base64-encoded blobs; schema is an IETF-style short identifier (e.g., "redwood.v1.chat.turn").

2) Fragment types: the runtime must recognize at minimum: CONTENT_FRAME, TOOL_CALL, TOOL_RESULT, CHECKPOINT, HEARTBEAT, ERROR_FRAME. Each type has deterministic merging behaviour described below.

3) Tool/function invocation semantics:
- TOOL_CALL frames act as an outbound RPC request from the LLM to an external tool gateway. TOOL_CALL includes a call_id and an idempotency_key (both opaque).
- The runtime MUST guarantee exactly-once delivery of TOOL_CALL to the configured tool gateway within the current routing policy or, if unreachable, emit a TOOL_CALL_REJECTED frame with retryable=false/true flag and rejection_reason.
- TOOL_RESULT frames with matching call_id may arrive later and MUST be applied to the parent fragment by client/consumer code. If TOOL_RESULT replays are received (duplicate call_id), they must be de-duplicated using idempotency_key.

4) Checkpoints and partial reconciliation:
- CHECKPOINT frames represent persisted byte offsets and a canonical snapshot id. Clients MAY use CHECKPOINTs to truncate local replays and mark safe commit points.
- On reconnect, the runtime must supply missing frames since last known checkpoint when possible. If frames exceed retention window, runtime must emit a TRUNCATION_NOTICE with last_known_checkpoint and a recovery_hint.

5) Streaming boundaries and finalization:
- is_final=true on an envelope signals logical completion for that stream. Consumers must not assume content immutability until a final checkpoint or is_final.
- In the presence of network partition, partial frames MAY be emitted; the runtime must emit HEARTBEAT frames every 5s of silence to avoid client stalls (configurable).

6) Error taxonomy and repair guidance:
- Transient errors (network, temporary tool error): emit ERROR_FRAME with transient=true and suggested_retry_seconds. Resume semantics: runtime will attempt automated retry up to N times (configurable) then emit TOOL_CALL_REJECTED with transient=false.
- Permanent errors (schema mismatch, auth): transient=false and include mitigation steps in the payload.
- Corrupted frames (invalid JSON, checksum mismatch): runtime must attempt best-effort repair: 1) request a resend for that seq_id, 2) mark affected checkpoint invalid if repair fails, 3) emit CORRUPTION_NOTICE and move stream to degraded mode.

7) Observability and SLOs for acceptance:
- Each stream must surface the following metrics per-minute: frames_emitted, frames_retransmitted, tool_calls_issued, tool_call_latency_p95, tool_call_failures_by_reason, reconnections, truncations.
- Tracing must correlate call_id -> request_id -> trace_id. Console UX must show the last 20 frames for each stream and emphasize CHECKPOINTs and TOOL_CALLs.

8) Backpressure and flow-control:
- The runtime must support a simple credit-based flow control header: credits_granted on the CONNECT response. If credits are exhausted, runtime must buffer up to buffer_limit (configurable) and then apply policy: drop_oldest | reject_new (configurable per-tenant). Acceptance requires tests for both policies.

9) Security and privacy constraints:
- TOOL_CALL and TOOL_RESULT frames must support envelope-level encryption (optional per-deployment). Acceptance requires that private deployment tests demonstrate KMS-encrypted TOOL_RESULT payloads can be decrypted end-to-end by the configured HSM/KMS.

10) Backwards compatibility and graceful evolution:
- When payload_schema changes, runtime must support schema negotiation via a SCHEMA_ANNOUNCE frame with migration_hint. Clients that receive unknown schema identifiers must be able to follow a defined fallback: 1) attempt best-effort parsing as generic map, 2) emit SCHEMA_ERROR (non-fatal) and continue if allowed by config. Acceptance includes a compatibility test between runtime-2.3 (no payload_schema header) and runtime-2.4 where schema is optional.

Detailed test cases (to be codified in e2e tests):
A) Happy path: small chat turn with CONTENT_FRAME frames interleaving a TOOL_CALL and receiving TOOL_RESULT; final CHECKPOINT emitted; client reapplies frames successfully after reconnection.
B) Tool delayed: TOOL_CALL is delivered, network partition causes delayed TOOL_RESULT; runtime emits HEARTBEAT frames and then TOOL_RESULT; client de-dupes replays.
C) Tool gateway down: runtime emits TOOL_CALL_REJECTED with retryable=true then later replays TOOL_CALL when gateway recovered and emits TOOL_RESULT; check idempotency.
D) Truncation: client reconnects after retention window; assert TRUNCATION_NOTICE + recovery_hint delivered and console surfaces degrade state.
E) Corruption: runtime detects invalid JSON in a CONTENT_FRAME, tries resend; when resend fails, emits CORRUPTION_NOTICE and stream remains readable but degraded.
F) Backpressure policy: simulate high-rate emitter and validate both drop_oldest and reject_new behaviours against SLOs.

Operational runbooks (summary):
- On TOOL_CALL failure spikes: identify gateway cluster, increase retries threshold for canary traffic, open support ticket with gateway team.
- On high frame retransmits: evaluate kernel scheduling & batching metrics, consider increasing credits_granted per connection.
- On frequent truncations: check storage retention windows and adjust per-tenant retention or add streaming persistence.

Acceptance checklist (yes/no):
- [ ] Frame headers emitted and validated in runtime unit tests
- [ ] TOOL_CALL/TOOL_RESULT idempotency enforced in gateway integration tests
- [ ] Checkpoint resume tests passing for hosted and private deployments
- [ ] Corruption and resend paths covered by e2e failure injection tests
- [ ] Flow-control/backpressure policies have deterministic tests and per-tenant configs
- [ ] Metrics and traces available in console for sampled streams
- [ ] Security/KMS encrypted tool payload verified in staging (private deployment)

Notes and trade-offs:
- We opt for a compact ASCII header set to keep wire compatibility with existing streaming channels; more expressive OpenAPI-style envelopes can be added later but would need explicit migration.
- Exactly-once semantics for TOOL_CALLs at the runtime boundary is expensive; we target "delivery-at-most-once + idempotent-processing" for most internal gateways and require idempotency_key for true de-duplication when external tools may re-run calls.

Next steps:
- Engineering: implement runtime frame headers and basic CHECKPOINT resume (ENG-98012).
- QA: translate test cases into the streaming-e2e harness and add fault injection scenarios.
- Design/Console: display frame timeline and checkpoint markers in the stream inspector (DES-4402).
